title: Rate Limiting
summary: Cap how much any one caller may consume, so that one client cannot degrade the service for everyone else.
analogy: A nightclub with a capacity limit and a doorman. Not because the club dislikes people, but because past a certain number nobody inside has a good evening. The doorman also stops one large group taking the whole floor while everyone else queues outside.

explanation.beginner: Without a limit, one buggy script or one abusive user can send so many requests that your servers have nothing left for everyone else. A rate limiter counts requests per user (or per IP, or per API key) and rejects those beyond the allowance with status 429, usually with a header telling the caller when to try again. It protects you from accidents as much as from attacks — a retry loop with no backoff is the most common cause of self-inflicted outages.
explanation.interview: Admission control at the edge. Token bucket is the usual choice: tokens refill at a constant rate up to a burst capacity, giving a sustained rate with controlled burstiness in O(1) state per key. Fixed windows are simplest but allow 2x the limit across a boundary; sliding-window log is exact but O(requests) memory; sliding-window counter approximates it cheaply. Distributed enforcement needs shared state (Redis with atomic INCR or a Lua script) and must decide fail-open versus fail-closed when that store is unavailable.

nodes.label: Rate limiter\n(token bucket)
nodes.note: Checked before any real work. Rejecting costs microseconds; serving costs milliseconds.

without: One client at 10,000 rps consumes the capacity of all the others
A retry storm turns a blip into an outage
with: Each caller gets a predictable share
Excess is rejected cheaply, with a Retry-After hint
why.conclusion: Rate limiting is how a service protects its own availability from its callers — including from itself.

nodes.label: Redis\n(shared counters)
nodes.note: Needed when several limiter instances must enforce one global budget. Atomic INCR or a Lua script keeps it race-free.

without: A single client can saturate the service
Infrastructure cost tracks abuse rather than usage
Retry storms amplify small failures into full outages
No protection against credential stuffing or scraping
with: A lever to enforce plan tiers
Back-pressure that clients can actually respond to
why.conclusion: Every public endpoint needs a limit. The interesting question is which algorithm and at what granularity.

whenToUse: Expensive endpoints: search, report generation, anything hitting a third party
Login and OTP endpoints, to blunt credential stuffing
whenNotToUse: Internal, trusted, low-volume calls where a circuit breaker is the better protection
As a substitute for capacity — a limit set far below real demand is just a slower outage
Health checks and monitoring endpoints, which should be exempt

pros: Allows bursts up to the bucket size while capping the sustained rate
O(1) state per key: tokens plus a timestamp
cons: Bursts can still briefly exceed the average

pros: Trivial: one counter per key per window
cons: Boundary problem — a client can send the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next, doubling the intended rate
Stores a timestamp per request; memory grows with traffic, which is itself a denial-of-service vector

pros: Close to exact with two counters and a weighted estimate
cons: An approximation; slightly wrong during bursts

pros: Perfectly smooth output rate, protects fragile downstreams
cons: No burst allowance, which feels unfair to well-behaved bursty clients

keyNumbers.label: Token bucket state
keyNumbers.value: 2 values per key — tokens and last refill time

quiz.question: With a fixed window of 100 requests per minute, how many requests can a client make in a two-second span?
options: 200 — 100 at the end of one window and 100 at the start of the next
quiz.explanation: The boundary problem. Sliding window or token bucket smooths this out, which is why fixed windows are rarely used where the limit really matters.

quiz.question: Your Redis instance backing a distributed rate limiter goes down. Fail open or fail closed?
options: It is a deliberate trade: fail open keeps the service usable but unprotected; fail closed protects the backend but causes an outage. Most public APIs fail open with local per-instance fallback limits
Always fail open with no fallback
quiz.explanation: There is no universally right answer, and being able to argue both sides is the point. The usual compromise is fail open globally while each instance applies a conservative local limit.

quiz.question: Why is token bucket usually preferred over leaky bucket for public APIs?
options: It permits short bursts up to the bucket size while still capping the sustained rate, which matches how legitimate clients actually behave
quiz.explanation: Real clients are bursty — a page load fires ten requests at once. A leaky bucket would smooth that into a queue and feel sluggish; a token bucket absorbs it as long as the average stays within budget.
